summary: Describes using keyed SHA with the IP Authentication Header to provide integrity and authentication for IP datagrams. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 2841.

eli5.summary: A secret-ingredient fingerprint recipe, using a hashing method called SHA, for showing a packet is real.

subtitle: Using SHA hashing to authenticate IP packets with a secret key.

tldr.problem: The IP Authentication Header (AH) needs a cryptographic algorithm to compute integrity checks. MD5 was widely used, but implementers wanted alternatives, particularly ones that did not require proprietary licensing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1852 specifies how to use the SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) with a secret key as the algorithm for computing AH authentication digests. The secret key and datagram are hashed together to produce a 160-bit authentication value that verifies both that a packet has not been altered and that it came from someone with the shared secret key.
tldr.outcome: SHA became an alternative for IP authentication, though MD5 remained more common due to performance. SHA was later incorporated into broader IPsec specifications and eventually obsoleted by RFC 2841 as security practices evolved.

facts.label: Key length support
facts.value: Up to 160 bits minimum, longer encouraged

today: RFC 1852 is experimental and was superseded by RFC 2841. It represents an early approach to IP authentication using SHA. Today, IPsec authentication has evolved significantly, with stronger algorithms and integration into comprehensive security protocols. SHA itself remains widely used, though stronger variants like SHA-256 are now standard.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1852 describes the use of keyed SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) with the IP Authentication Header (AH), as defined in RFC 1826. The AH provides integrity and authentication for IP datagrams by computing a cryptographic checksum that covers the entire packet.

This RFC assumes familiarity with RFC 1825 (Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol), which provides the security framework. It specifies a corrected version of SHA, as the original SHA specification (FIPS-180) was discovered to have a flaw. At the time of writing, SHA had no known attacks better than brute force, and its 160-bit output size offered stronger resistance to brute force than the 128-bit algorithms like MD4 and MD5.
sections.eli5: This explains how to use SHA, a secure mixing method, to create a fingerprint of a network packet that proves it is real and unchanged.

sections.title: Keys and Data Sizing
sections.content:
The RFC requires that the secret authentication key shared between communicating parties be a cryptographically strong random number, not a guessable string. The key length is not constrained by the transform itself, though implementations must support keys up to 160 bits, and longer keys are encouraged.

SHA's 160-bit output is naturally 32-bit aligned, but many systems require 64-bit alignment of following headers. In such cases, an additional 32 bits of padding is added, either before or after the SHA output. The size and position of padding are negotiated as part of key management. Padding bits are filled with implementation-dependent random values that are ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: You share a secret key with the other computer. The longer the key, the better. Padding is added to make everything line up properly in memory.

sections.title: Computing the Digest
sections.content:
The 160-bit SHA digest is calculated per FIPS 180-1. The authenticated message takes the form: key, keyfill, datagram, key, SHAfill.

First, the variable-length secret key is padded to the next 512-bit boundary using SHA's standard padding technique. The padded key is concatenated with the entire IP datagram (with variant fields zeroed), then concatenated with the original key again. Finally, SHA adds its own trailing padding to reach the next 512-bit boundary and computes the 160-bit digest. The digest is inserted into the Authentication Data field of the AH.

The design uses the key twice (at the beginning and end) to provide protection for the entire datagram and minimal protection against attacks on the IP length field. The leading padded key facilitates efficient copying at machine boundaries without realignment.
sections.eli5: The recipe mixes the secret key, then the packet, then the key again, creating a fingerprint hash that proves the packet came from someone with that key.

sections.title: Performance and Strength
sections.content:
Preliminary performance analysis showed that SHA is approximately 62% as fast as MD5, and 80% as fast as DES-based hashing (MD5 being fastest, DES intermediate, and SHA slowest). This performance trade-off meant that while SHA was more secure due to its larger hash size, implementations often chose MD5 for better throughput.

The RFC notes that the security of this approach depends entirely on several factors: the strength of the SHA algorithm itself, the correctness of its implementation, the security of the key management mechanism, the strength of the shared key, and the correctness of implementations in all participating nodes. Users need to understand that any weakness in any of these components can compromise the authentication provided.
sections.eli5: SHA is slower than some other methods but provides strong security. Its strength depends on having a good secret key and correct implementation.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
At the time of writing, no known attacks on SHA existed better than brute force, making it significantly more resistant than 128-bit hashes. However, the RFC cautions that cryptographers can be fallible: the original SHA specification had to be corrected in FIPS 180-1, and there may be substantial deficiencies yet to be discovered.

The document notes that a flaw was found in the original SHA (FIPS-180), which is not interoperable with the corrected version specified here. The RFC requests comments on alternative authentication algorithms that are faster, not patent-encumbered, and still retain adequate cryptographic strength. This document marks one point in the evolution of IPsec authentication, before the field consolidated on stronger approaches.
sections.eli5: SHA is secure for now, but cryptography changes as computers get faster. This method was later replaced with even stronger ones.
